questions.questionText: What is the difference between a StatelessWidget and a StatefulWidget?

options.text: StatelessWidget has a BuildContext, StatefulWidget does not
StatelessWidget never rebuilds; StatefulWidget can rebuild when its State changes
StatelessWidget is faster and should always be used
StatefulWidget is only for screens, not for small widgets

questions.explanation: A StatelessWidget describes a part of the user interface that can depend only on the configuration information in the object itself and the BuildContext. A StatefulWidget is associated with a State object that can rebuild the widget tree by calling setState().

questions.questionText: Which method is called when Flutter needs to build the widget tree for a StatelessWidget?

options.text: init()
render()
build(BuildContext context)
create()

questions.explanation: The build() method is the only required method in a StatelessWidget (and StatefulWidget's State). Flutter calls it whenever the widget needs to be rendered or re-rendered.

questions.questionText: What does calling setState() do in a StatefulWidget?

options.text: Immediately updates the UI synchronously
Marks the widget as dirty and schedules a rebuild on the next frame
Reloads the entire app
Sends a signal to the parent widget

questions.explanation: setState() marks the State object as dirty and schedules a rebuild. Flutter batches rebuilds and processes them on the next frame, making it efficient even when setState() is called multiple times.

questions.questionText: Which of the following are correct about the Flutter widget tree? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Every Flutter app has a widget tree, element tree, and render tree
Widgets are immutable descriptions of the UI
Changing a widget's properties modifies the existing widget object
Elements are long-lived objects that hold widget configuration

questions.explanation: Flutter maintains three trees: widgets (immutable blueprints), elements (long-lived managers), and render objects (layout & painting). Widgets are immutable — you create new widget objects rather than mutating them. Elements persist across rebuilds and reconcile widget changes.

questions.questionText: What is a BuildContext in Flutter?

options.text: A handle to the location of a widget in the widget tree
A configuration object for the build system
The root of the entire app widget tree
An object that manages state changes

questions.explanation: BuildContext is a handle to the location of a widget in the widget tree. It provides access to the theme, media query, inherited widgets, and other tree-level information. Each widget receives its own BuildContext in the build() method.

questions.questionText: Which widget is used to display a scrollable list of children that are created on demand?

options.text: Column
ListView.builder
GridView
Stack

questions.explanation: ListView.builder creates list items lazily — only those visible on screen are built. This makes it ideal for long or infinite lists. Column renders all children at once regardless of visibility.

questions.questionText: What is the purpose of the Key parameter in widgets?

options.text: To assign a unique ID for database storage
To help Flutter identify which widgets in the tree have changed during reconciliation
To provide accessibility labels
To encrypt widget data

questions.explanation: Keys help Flutter identify widgets during the reconciliation process when the widget tree changes. They are especially important when reordering a list of stateful widgets, ensuring the correct State is associated with the correct widget.

questions.questionText: Which lifecycle method in a StatefulWidget's State is called when the widget is first inserted into the tree?

options.text: build()
didUpdateWidget()
initState()
activate()

questions.explanation: initState() is called exactly once when the State object is created and inserted into the tree. It is the correct place to initialize state, subscribe to streams, or set up animations. Always call super.initState() first.

questions.questionText: What widget wraps a child and gives it an explicit width and height? (Enter the widget name)
questions.explanation: SizedBox is used to give a widget a specific size. It creates a box with specific dimensions. SizedBox.shrink() creates a zero-size box, and SizedBox.expand() fills all available space.

questions.questionText: What does the Expanded widget do inside a Row or Column?

options.text: It makes the child widget bigger than its natural size
It causes the child to take up all remaining available space along the main axis
It adds padding around the child widget
It makes the Row or Column scrollable

questions.explanation: Expanded causes its child to fill all remaining space along the main axis of a Flex widget (Row or Column). Multiple Expanded widgets share the available space according to their flex factors.

questions.questionText: What does the '?' symbol mean when used after a type declaration in Dart (e.g., String?)?

options.text: The variable is optional and may not be declared
The variable is nullable and can hold a null value
The variable requires a default value
It is a conditional declaration

questions.explanation: In Dart's null safety system, 'String?' means the variable can hold either a String value or null. Without the '?', the type is non-nullable and must always have a non-null value. Null safety was introduced in Dart 2.12.

questions.questionText: What is the output of: print(5 ~/ 2); in Dart?

options.text: Error

questions.explanation: The ~/ operator in Dart is the integer division (truncating division) operator. 5 ~/ 2 gives 2 (not 2.5). For floating point division use / which gives 2.5.

questions.questionText: What keyword is used to declare a variable whose value will not change after initialization?

options.text: static
fixed
final
immutable

questions.explanation: The 'final' keyword means the variable can only be set once. The 'const' keyword is stricter — it means the value must be a compile-time constant. Use 'final' when the value is set at runtime but won't change thereafter.

questions.questionText: Which of the following are true about async/await in Dart? (Select all that apply)

options.text: An async function always returns a Future
await can only be used inside an async function
await blocks the entire Dart thread
async/await is syntactic sugar over Future chaining

questions.explanation: async functions always return a Future (even if you return a non-Future value, it's wrapped). await can only be used in async functions. Crucially, await does NOT block the thread — it suspends the current function and lets the event loop process other events. async/await is indeed syntactic sugar over Future.then() chains.

questions.questionText: What is a mixin in Dart?

options.text: A type of abstract class that cannot be instantiated
A way to reuse a class's code in multiple class hierarchies without inheritance
A special constructor that blends multiple classes
An interface that requires implementing all methods

questions.explanation: Mixins allow you to reuse code across multiple class hierarchies without traditional inheritance. A class uses a mixin with the 'with' keyword. Dart's mixin system solves the 'diamond problem' of multiple inheritance by linearizing the mixin application.

questions.questionText: What is the '??' operator in Dart called and what does it do?

options.text: Double-null; throws an error if both sides are null
Null-coalescing; returns the left operand if non-null, otherwise the right
Null-check; throws if the value is null
Null-assertion; forces a nullable type to non-null

questions.explanation: ?? is the null-coalescing operator. 'expr1 ?? expr2' evaluates to expr1 if it is non-null, otherwise evaluates and returns expr2. It's useful for providing default values: String name = input ?? 'Default';

questions.questionText: What is the difference between 'const' and 'final' in Dart?

options.text: There is no difference; they are interchangeable
const must be a compile-time constant; final is set once at runtime
final must be a compile-time constant; const is set once at runtime
const is for primitives only; final is for objects

questions.explanation: const requires the value to be known at compile time (e.g., const pi = 3.14;). final allows the value to be determined at runtime but can only be set once (e.g., final now = DateTime.now();). const objects are canonicalized — identical const values share the same instance.

questions.questionText: What does the 'late' keyword do in Dart null safety?

options.text: Declares a variable that is initialized asynchronously
Declares a non-nullable variable that will be initialized before first use
Makes a final variable settable multiple times
Delays compilation of a variable declaration

questions.explanation: The 'late' keyword tells Dart that a non-nullable variable will be initialized before it is first read. If it is read before being initialized, a LateInitializationError is thrown at runtime. It's commonly used for non-nullable fields that can't be set in the constructor.

questions.questionText: What Dart collection type stores key-value pairs? (Enter the type name)
questions.explanation: A Map is a collection of key-value pairs where each key is unique. Dart Maps can be created with literals: {'key': 'value'} or Map<String, int>(). Common operations include map[key], map.containsKey(), map.entries, and map.forEach().

questions.questionText: What is a Stream in Dart?

options.text: A single asynchronous value that completes once
A sequence of asynchronous events over time
A data structure for high-performance I/O
A type of Future that can be cancelled

questions.explanation: A Stream is a sequence of asynchronous events (similar to an asynchronous Iterable). You can listen to a Stream with stream.listen(), or use async/await with 'await for'. Streams can be single-subscription or broadcast (multiple listeners).

questions.questionText: In Riverpod, what is the difference between ref.watch() and ref.read()?

options.text: watch() reads once; read() subscribes to changes
watch() subscribes and rebuilds on change; read() reads once without subscribing
They are functionally identical
read() is for async providers; watch() is for sync providers

questions.explanation: ref.watch() subscribes to the provider and causes the widget or provider to rebuild whenever the value changes. ref.read() reads the current value exactly once without subscribing. Use watch() in build() and provider bodies; use read() in event handlers and callbacks.

questions.questionText: What type of provider would you use for state that can be mutated over time in Riverpod?

options.text: Provider
FutureProvider
StateNotifierProvider
StreamProvider

questions.explanation: StateNotifierProvider pairs with a StateNotifier class. The StateNotifier holds the current state and exposes methods to mutate it. The provider exposes the current state value and rebuilds watchers when state changes. This is the recommended pattern for mutable state in Riverpod.

questions.questionText: What is ProviderScope in Riverpod?

options.text: A widget that defines which providers are available to its subtree
A class that limits which widgets can access a provider
A debug tool for inspecting provider state
An annotation for generating providers

questions.explanation: ProviderScope is a widget that must wrap your entire app (usually at the root). It stores the state of all Riverpod providers. It can also be used to override providers for testing or to scope providers to a subtree.

questions.questionText: Which of the following are valid ways to listen to a provider in Riverpod? (Select all that apply)

options.text: ref.watch() in a ConsumerWidget build()
ref.listen() to execute a callback on change
ref.read() to subscribe to all future changes
ref.watch() inside another provider

questions.explanation: ref.watch() in build() rebuilds the widget on change. ref.listen() registers a callback (useful for navigation, showing dialogs). ref.watch() inside a provider creates a dependency. ref.read() does NOT subscribe to changes — it's a one-time read, not a way to listen.

questions.questionText: What is InheritedWidget used for in Flutter?

options.text: To create widgets that inherit layout properties from their parent
To efficiently propagate data down the widget tree
To inherit themes from the MaterialApp
To extend StatefulWidget with extra capabilities

questions.explanation: InheritedWidget is a low-level mechanism for sharing data down the widget tree without passing it through every constructor. Provider, Theme, MediaQuery, and Navigator are all built on InheritedWidget. When the InheritedWidget's data changes, only dependent widgets rebuild.

questions.questionText: When should you use ValueNotifier over StateNotifier in Flutter?

options.text: ValueNotifier is always better and should replace StateNotifier
For simple single-value state with no complex logic; StateNotifier is better for complex state machines
ValueNotifier is for async state; StateNotifier is for sync state
They are functionally identical

questions.explanation: ValueNotifier<T> is a simple ChangeNotifier that holds a single value and notifies listeners when it changes. It's great for simple local state. StateNotifier is more powerful for complex state machines with explicit state transitions via typed methods.

questions.questionText: What does AsyncValue represent in Riverpod?

options.text: A nullable Future value
A union type representing loading, error, or data states of an async operation
A provider that automatically retries on error
A Stream converted to a Future

questions.explanation: AsyncValue<T> is a union type with three states: AsyncLoading (operation in progress), AsyncError (failed with an error and stack trace), and AsyncData<T> (succeeded with a value). FutureProvider and StreamProvider expose AsyncValue. Use .when() to handle all three states cleanly.

questions.questionText: What is the correct place to call ref.read() in a ConsumerWidget?

options.text: At the top of the build() method
Inside event handlers and callbacks, not in build()
In the widget constructor
Inside a FutureBuilder

questions.explanation: ref.read() should be used inside callbacks and event handlers (e.g., onPressed). Using ref.read() in build() works but is discouraged because it won't cause rebuilds when the value changes. Use ref.watch() for reactive reads in build().

questions.questionText: What method on StateNotifier is used to update the state? (Enter the property name)
questions.explanation: In a StateNotifier, you update the state by assigning to the 'state' property: state = newValue;. The StateNotifier automatically notifies all listeners when state is set to a new value. Never mutate the existing state object directly — always create a new instance.

questions.questionText: What is the purpose of ref.invalidate() in Riverpod?

options.text: Permanently disables a provider from being used
Forces a provider to re-run its initialization logic on the next read
Removes a provider from the ProviderScope
Cancels any pending async operations in a FutureProvider

questions.explanation: ref.invalidate() marks a provider as stale so it will be re-initialized on the next time it is accessed. This is useful for refreshing data (like re-fetching from an API) without permanently destroying the provider's state.

questions.questionText: What is the difference between mainAxisAlignment and crossAxisAlignment in a Row?

options.text: mainAxisAlignment controls horizontal alignment; crossAxisAlignment controls vertical alignment
They are interchangeable
mainAxisAlignment controls vertical alignment; crossAxisAlignment controls horizontal alignment
mainAxisAlignment only works in Column; crossAxisAlignment only works in Row

questions.explanation: In a Row, the main axis is horizontal, so mainAxisAlignment controls horizontal positioning. The cross axis is vertical, so crossAxisAlignment controls vertical positioning. In a Column these are reversed: mainAxisAlignment is vertical, crossAxisAlignment is horizontal.

questions.questionText: What widget should you use to make a widget fill all available space in both directions?

options.text: Expanded
Flexible
SizedBox.expand()
Container(width: double.infinity, height: double.infinity)

questions.explanation: SizedBox.expand() creates a SizedBox that expands to fill all available space in both dimensions. Expanded only works in Row/Column flex contexts. Container with infinite dimensions may cause layout errors if there are no constraints from the parent.

questions.questionText: Which widget allows you to place children on top of each other?

options.text: Column
Overlay
Stack
IndexedStack

questions.explanation: Stack places children on top of each other. Children are positioned using Positioned widgets within the Stack. The last child in the children list is drawn on top. IndexedStack is a subclass of Stack that shows only one child at a time by index.

questions.questionText: Which of the following are standard implicit animation widgets in Flutter? (Select all that apply)

options.text: AnimatedContainer
AnimatedOpacity
TweenAnimationBuilder
AnimatedBuilder

questions.explanation: AnimatedContainer and AnimatedOpacity are implicit animation widgets — they animate automatically between old and new property values. TweenAnimationBuilder is also implicit, taking a Tween and animating to the target value. AnimatedBuilder is an explicit animation widget that requires an AnimationController.

questions.questionText: What is MediaQuery used for in Flutter?

options.text: Playing media files (video and audio)
Accessing device information like screen size, orientation, and text scale factor
Fetching images from the internet
Querying the device's sensor data

questions.explanation: MediaQuery.of(context) provides information about the device's screen and system settings: size, orientation, devicePixelRatio, padding (safe areas), textScaleFactor, and more. Use MediaQuery.sizeOf(context) in Flutter 3.10+ for better performance.

questions.questionText: What is the purpose of the SafeArea widget?

options.text: To prevent widgets from being tapped accidentally
To add padding that avoids system intrusions like notches and home indicators
To prevent sensitive data from appearing in screenshots
To add rounded corners to a widget

questions.explanation: SafeArea insets its child by the appropriate amount to avoid intrusions from the operating system: status bar, notch, home indicator, and navigation bar. It uses MediaQuery.of(context).padding internally. Always wrap screen content in SafeArea to handle notches.

questions.questionText: What is a CustomPainter used for in Flutter?

options.text: Applying custom colors to existing Material widgets
Drawing arbitrary graphics directly to a canvas with low-level drawing APIs
Creating custom widget layouts using rows and columns
Customizing the app's theme painter

questions.explanation: CustomPainter gives you direct access to the Canvas, allowing you to draw any shape, path, text, or image using methods like drawLine(), drawRect(), drawPath(), and drawImage(). It's used with the CustomPaint widget and is ideal for charts, custom shapes, and game rendering.

questions.questionText: Which widget enables a smooth scrollable list where items are built lazily?

options.text: Column with SingleChildScrollView
ListView.builder
Wrap
Flow

questions.explanation: ListView.builder is the correct choice for long or infinite lists. Items are built on demand as the user scrolls. A Column with SingleChildScrollView renders ALL children at once, which is inefficient for long lists.

questions.questionText: What Flutter widget clips its child to a circular shape? (Enter the widget name)
questions.explanation: ClipOval clips its child widget to an oval (or circle if the child is square). CircleAvatar also creates circular images but with a specific avatar design. ClipOval is the general-purpose clipping widget for circular clips.

questions.questionText: What is the purpose of RepaintBoundary in Flutter?

options.text: Prevents a widget from being repainted when its parent repaints
Creates a visual boundary line around a widget
Limits the area in which touch events are detected
Prevents repainting of widgets outside the viewport

questions.explanation: RepaintBoundary creates a separate layer for its child, so repainting the child doesn't cause the parent (or siblings) to repaint, and vice versa. It's a performance optimization useful for widgets that animate independently, like a live chart or a video player.

questions.questionText: In Clean Architecture, what is the correct direction of dependency?

options.text: Domain depends on Data; Data depends on Presentation
Presentation depends on Domain; Domain never depends on outer layers
All layers are independent and don't depend on each other
Data depends on Domain; Presentation depends on Data

questions.explanation: In Clean Architecture, dependencies point inward: Presentation → Domain (via use cases) and Data → Domain (implements domain interfaces). The Domain layer is the innermost and most stable — it has zero dependencies on outer layers, making it independently testable.

questions.questionText: What does GoRouter's redirect function do?

options.text: Permanently replaces one route with another in the route table
Intercepts navigation and optionally redirects to a different route based on app state
Forwards HTTP requests to a different URL
Resets the navigation stack to the initial route

questions.explanation: GoRouter's redirect callback is called on every navigation attempt. Returning a non-null string redirects to that route; returning null allows the navigation to proceed. It's the correct place to implement auth guards, onboarding checks, and other navigation-level logic.

questions.questionText: What is the purpose of the Repository pattern in Flutter apps?

options.text: Storing code in version control repositories
Abstracting data sources behind a single interface to decouple business logic from data fetching details
Caching network responses on disk
Providing a global registry of singleton objects

questions.explanation: The Repository pattern abstracts where data comes from (network, local database, cache) behind a clean interface. The domain layer calls the repository interface without knowing whether data comes from an API or local storage. This makes testing easy — swap the real repo with a fake one.

questions.questionText: Which of the following are recommended Flutter testing approaches? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Unit tests for business logic and models
Widget tests for UI components in isolation
Integration tests for full user flows on a real device or emulator
Manual testing only — automated tests are not needed for mobile

questions.explanation: Flutter supports three levels of testing: unit tests (fast, test logic in isolation), widget tests (test UI widgets with a simulated Flutter engine), and integration tests (run on a real device or emulator, test full flows). All three complement each other and are recommended.

questions.questionText: What is dependency injection and why is it useful in Flutter?

options.text: A way to inject CSS styles into Flutter widgets
Providing dependencies to classes from outside rather than creating them internally, enabling testability
A method to inject code at runtime using reflection
Automatically importing packages based on usage

questions.explanation: Dependency injection means providing a class with its dependencies externally (via constructor, property, or a DI framework) rather than having it create them. This makes code more testable (inject mocks), more flexible, and loosely coupled. Riverpod, GetIt, and injectable are common DI approaches in Flutter.

questions.questionText: What does the 'flutter analyze' command do?

options.text: Runs all unit and widget tests
Analyzes Dart code for errors, warnings, and style violations using the analyzer
Analyzes app performance and memory usage
Checks for outdated packages in pubspec.yaml

questions.explanation: flutter analyze runs the Dart static analyzer on your project. It reports errors (code that won't compile), warnings (potential issues), and lint suggestions (style rules from analysis_options.yaml). Running it as part of CI ensures code quality standards are maintained.

questions.questionText: What is the purpose of pubspec.yaml in a Flutter project?

options.text: Configuring build scripts for Android and iOS
Declaring the app's name, version, dependencies, and assets
Storing app secrets and API keys
Defining the widget tree structure

questions.explanation: pubspec.yaml is the manifest file for a Dart/Flutter project. It declares: the app name and description, the SDK version constraints, all package dependencies (with versions), dev dependencies, and Flutter-specific config like asset paths and font declarations.

questions.questionText: What does GoRouter's ShellRoute do?

options.text: Adds a shell script execution capability to Flutter apps
Wraps child routes in a shared widget (like a bottom nav bar) that persists across navigation
Creates a nested navigation stack that operates independently
Provides a terminal-like debug interface for navigation

questions.explanation: ShellRoute wraps its child routes in a persistent shared widget — typically a Scaffold with a bottom navigation bar. When navigating between shell routes, the shell widget stays mounted while only the body (child) changes, avoiding rebuilds of the navigation bar.

questions.questionText: What command installs new packages listed in pubspec.yaml? (Enter the full command without 'flutter ')
questions.explanation: Running 'flutter pub get' downloads and installs all packages listed in pubspec.yaml and updates pubspec.lock. Always run this after modifying pubspec.yaml or when cloning a project for the first time.

questions.questionText: What is tree shaking in the context of Flutter/Dart compilation?

options.text: Removing unused widgets from the widget tree at runtime
Eliminating unused code during compilation to reduce the final app size
A garbage collection algorithm for the Dart VM
Removing broken branches from the dependency tree

questions.explanation: Tree shaking is a dead-code elimination technique performed by the Dart compiler during release builds. Code (functions, classes, constants) that is never referenced is removed from the final binary, significantly reducing app size. This is one reason why importing unused packages still has a size cost.
